\chapter{Taking Your Leave}
\label{ch:sa-leave-more}
\hlchaptermodality{28}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can take my leave in Sanskrit, wish someone a good journey, and take the old farewell apart into the two words that built it.}

Complete SA-C28-svasti and demonstrate the chapter promise.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[idānīm]{\sk{इदानीम्} (idānīm) — now}

\label{lesson:SA-C28-now}



\begin{quote}
Before the new word: what did \emph{evam} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{इदानीम्}}
\textbf{\sk{इदानीम्}} (\emph{idānīm}) — \textquotedblleft{}now\textquotedblright{}.

\textbf{\sk{इदानीम्}} is \emph{now}. It belongs with \sk{सदा}, \sk{अद्य} and \sk{ह्यः} — always, today, yesterday — and it is the sharpest of them: not this day, this moment.

It is built on the near-pointing stem you met with \sk{एतत्}, \textquotedblleft{}this one\textquotedblright{}. The pointing system runs \emph{a-} / \emph{t-} / \emph{k-}, and \sk{इदानीम्} is the near end of it applied to time rather than to place: \emph{this}-time. \sk{गच्छामि} \sk{इदानीम्} — \textquotedblleft{}I am going now\textquotedblright{} — is a way to take your leave that reuses the verb you learned for exactly that purpose.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A time word built out of the pointing system, and a way to leave.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{idānīm}
  \item \emph{Say it:} it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{idānīm}, then \emph{gacchāmi idānīm} as one phrase
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{guruḥ}, then read \textbf{\sk{अस्तु}}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \sk{इदानीम्} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}now\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[paraśvaḥ]{\sk{परश्वः} (paraśvaḥ) — the day after tomorrow}

\label{lesson:SA-C28-day-after}



\begin{quote}
Before the new word: what did \emph{idānīm} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{परश्वः}}
\textbf{\sk{परश्वः}} (\emph{paraśvaḥ}) — \textquotedblleft{}the day after tomorrow\textquotedblright{}.

You have \textbf{\sk{श्वः}} (\emph{śvaḥ}), \textquotedblleft{}tomorrow\textquotedblright{}. \textbf{\sk{परश्वः}} is \emph{para} + \emph{śvaḥ}: the further tomorrow, the day after it.

English needs four words for this and Sanskrit needs one, because \emph{para} — \textquotedblleft{}beyond, further\textquotedblright{} — can be bolted onto the front of a time word. The same trick runs backwards from \sk{ह्यः}, yesterday, to give the day before it. So this is not really a new word to memorise; it is one you can assemble, which is the cheapest kind of vocabulary there is.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A word you could have built yourself out of two you had.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{paraśvaḥ}
  \item \emph{Say it:} it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{śvaḥ}, then \emph{paraśvaḥ}, and say what \emph{para} contributes
  \item \emph{Recall:} read \textbf{\sk{शिष्यः}}, then say \emph{sādhu}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \sk{परश्वः} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}the day after tomorrow\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[i]{\sk{इ} — one character, met inside words you already say}

\label{lesson:SA-S224-letter-i}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one, the ones you have already met: \sk{ओ} · \sk{फ} · \sk{◌ै}. Say what each of them does.

One character this time. One only — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script you'll notice: \sk{इ}}
\textbf{\sk{इ}} — \emph{i}.

It is an \textbf{independent vowel}: the full-size letter a vowel wears when it opens a word and has no consonant to lean on. Inside a word the same vowel is written as a small sign instead.

What it is made of:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item a descending upright joined to an upper bowl
  \item a lower bowl and diagonal tail in the same run
  \item the top shirorekhā
\end{itemize}

You already say these, and every one of them has \sk{इ} somewhere inside it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\sk{इदानीम्}} \emph{idānīm} — now
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Writing: \sk{इ}}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{1.} descend the upright from the headline, turn left around the upper bowl, sweep right through the waist and around the lower bowl, then finish down-right through the tail without lifting
  \item \textbf{2.} lift and draw the top shirorekhā left-to-right
\end{itemize}

\textbf{Pen lifts: 1.} The pen comes up 1 times and no more.

\begin{quote}
verified modern printed teaching form; everyday handwriting may simplify the curves
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
This is one attested teaching order and not a national standard — handwriting here is taught with school-to-school variation. Source: Saurmandal, ‘Devanagari \sk{इ} stroke order.svg’, panels 1–2, Wikimedia Commons, 5 August 2023.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Look:} at this, and find \sk{इ} in it
\end{itemize}

\begin{quote}
\sk{इदानीम्}
\end{quote}

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Trace it:} \sk{इ} three times, saying \emph{i} as you finish each one
  \item \emph{Look:} back at any page of this chapter and find \sk{इ} once more
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which character is this — \sk{इ}? What sound does it carry? (\emph{\textbf{i}}.) Name one word you already say that contains it.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[yātrā]{\sk{यात्रा} (yātrā) — a journey}

\label{lesson:SA-C28-journey}



\begin{quote}
Before the new word: what did \emph{paraśvaḥ} mean, and what did \emph{śvaḥ} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{यात्रा}}
\textbf{\sk{यात्रा}} (\emph{yātrā}) — \textquotedblleft{}a journey\textquotedblright{}.

\textbf{\sk{यात्रा}} is a journey — a going, and by long custom a going somewhere holy. Modern Indian languages kept it whole: a \emph{yatra} is a pilgrimage.

It comes from a root \emph{yā}, \textquotedblleft{}to go\textquotedblright{}, which is not the root behind \sk{गच्छति}. Sanskrit keeps several going-verbs apart, and this one leans toward setting out and travelling rather than the plain act of moving. Feminine, ending in \textbf{-\sk{आ}}, like \sk{माता} and \sk{नारी}.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A second going-root, and a noun made from it.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{yātrā}
  \item \emph{Say it:} it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{gacchati}, then \emph{yātrā}, and say which one sounds like setting out
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{rājā}, then read \textbf{\sk{अलम्}}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \sk{यात्रा} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}a journey\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[śubham]{\sk{शुभम्} (śubham) — good, auspicious}

\label{lesson:SA-C28-auspicious}



\begin{quote}
Before the new word: what did \emph{yātrā} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{शुभम्}}
\textbf{\sk{शुभम्}} (\emph{śubham}) — \textquotedblleft{}good, auspicious\textquotedblright{}.

You have \textbf{\sk{उत्तम}} (\emph{uttama}) for good in the sense of best. \textbf{\sk{शुभम्}} is good in the sense of \emph{auspicious} — bright, lucky, well-omened. Its root means \textquotedblleft{}to shine, to be beautiful\textquotedblright{}, so the word praises a thing for looking well rather than for being best.

It is a wishing word, and it goes in front of what you wish for. \textbf{\sk{शुभा} \sk{यात्रा}} — a good journey. \textbf{\sk{शुभा} \sk{रात्रिः}} — a good night. Both halves are already yours.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A wish you can attach to a journey or to a night.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{śubham}
  \item \emph{Say it:} it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{śubhā yātrā}, then \emph{śubhā rātriḥ}
  \item \emph{Recall:} read \textbf{\sk{अतिथिः}}, then say \emph{satyam}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \sk{शुभम्} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}good, auspicious\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[svasti]{\sk{स्वस्ति} (svasti) — well-being (may it go well)}

\label{lesson:SA-C28-svasti}



\begin{quote}
Before the last word of this run: what did \emph{śubham} mean, and what did \emph{idānīm} mean?
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \sk{स्वस्ति}}
\textbf{\sk{स्वस्ति}} (\emph{svasti}) — \textquotedblleft{}well-being (may it go well)\textquotedblright{}.

\textbf{\sk{स्वस्ति}} is the oldest farewell in this book, and you can take it apart with what you already have. \emph{Su-} means \textquotedblleft{}well\textquotedblright{} — it is the \emph{su-} inside \textbf{\sk{स्वागतम्}}, \textquotedblleft{}well-come\textquotedblright{}. \emph{Asti} means \textquotedblleft{}is\textquotedblright{}. So \sk{स्वस्ति} is, exactly, \textbf{it is well} — said as a wish over someone leaving.

Add the little ending \emph{-ka} and you have \emph{svastika}, \textquotedblleft{}the mark of well-being\textquotedblright{}, a good-luck sign that was drawn on doorways for thousands of years before the twentieth century took it and made it unusable in the West. The word is not the thing; but the word means what it means.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five ways to leave: now, the day after tomorrow, a journey, a good wish, and well-being itself.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{svasti}
  \item \emph{Say it:} it once more, slowly
  \item \emph{Say it:} all five in order, then take \emph{svasti} apart into its two pieces
  \item \emph{Recall:} say \emph{vaidyaḥ}, then read \textbf{\sk{एवम्}}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \sk{स्वस्ति} mean? (\textquotedblleft{}well-being (may it go well)\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
